title.narrative: Enhancing Conflict Sensitive and Reconciliation Practices in Fiji’s Security Sector

description.narrative:
Gender-based reform within the RFMF remains an ongoing challenge, as women in the security sector face systemic barriers to inclusion, limited representation in leadership, and exposure to workplace harassment and abuse. While some progress has been made, such as the recruitment of more female officers and discussions on gender policy reform, the pace of change remains slow, and structural inequalities persist. The military has acknowledged that gender equality efforts require further commitment, but without concrete institutional policies and enforcement mechanisms, meaningful progress remains limited.
The Fiji Police Force (FPF) has also played a significant role in shaping state-civil society relations, particularly in contexts of public unrest and insecurity. While the FPF has taken steps toward community engagement through the introduction of local policing committees and the establishment of community police posts, its approaches remain fragmented and lacking in trauma-informed approaches, particularly in high-risk rural areas and urban informal settlements. Past incidents of torture and excessive use of force have compounded public mistrust, especially among marginalised groups. Strengthening police-community relationships, improving institutional accountability, and embedding rights-based approaches are important to establish the FPF as a trusted public institution capable of contributing to long-term peace and democratic governance.
Security sector reform is a national priority embedded in Fiji’s policy frameworks and it is critical the security sector reflects on past interventions and adopts sustainable conflict-sensitive and gender-responsive practices. While both the military and police have expressed willingness to engage in reform, long-term support is essential to ensure these efforts are embedded and sustained.
